endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Responsibility for the oversight of areas like safety and security should rest high enough in the organization so that decisions can be made promptly about resources, risk mitigation, incident response, and potential rollback of AI systems

endorsements.title: Governing Generative AI in Healthcare: A Normative Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Authority, Trust, and the Architecture of Responsibility
endorsements.quote: Institutions must define escalation triggers in their deployment protocols.

endorsements.title: A conceptual multi-agent architecture for mental health triage in post-conflict Arabic-speaking populations: a theoretical proposition and staged validation argument
endorsements.quote: Incidents (missed crisis, harmful output, privacy breach, severe model failure) trigger immediate suspension of the affected agent pending review by a pre-constituted incident review panel (clinical lead, technical lead, ethics representative).

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether defined escalation pathways or designated suspension authority reduce the time unsafe AI tools stay in use, and no study documents how often that hazard occurs. Support for R252 rests on two CHAI frameworks and two commentaries, which describe expected practice without measuring outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The four endorsements are two frameworks and two commentaries, and one of the commentaries describes itself as a theoretical proposition. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion of this kind cannot be rated for certainty of effect, so the recommendation's support comes from consensus alone.

The endorsements describe a stop mechanism, with one commentary listing missed crisis, harmful output, privacy breach, and severe model failure as triggers for immediate suspension. No supplied study measures whether such triggers catch failures before patients are harmed, how often suspensions occur, or whether pausing a tool creates new risks when clinicians must revert to manual processes.

The CHAI guide places safety oversight high enough in the organization for prompt rollback decisions, which implies senior staff must be reachable for emergency review. No supplied study reports the staffing, on-call cost, or turnaround times of delegated or emergency review, so systems adopting R252 will need to set and track those measures themselves.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without designated suspension authority and measure time from incident detection to restriction of the tool, the number of patients exposed during that interval, and any disruption caused by pausing a tool. Descriptive incident audits that document how often unsafe AI remained in use for lack of an authorized decision maker would also establish whether the hazard occurs in practice.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One endorsing commentary addresses Arabic-speaking post-conflict populations, but it is a theoretical proposal without data, and it does not show whether suspension pathways work in under-resourced settings where senior reviewers may be scarce.
